Please read this carefully:

<document>
# A Cluster-Randomised Trial of a 30-Hour Week in Municipal Administration: Nine-Month Results

*Varden County Evaluation Unit, in collaboration with the Department of Labour Economics, Easterly University. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony and D. Rao. Registered protocol VC-2023-04.*

## Summary

We randomly assigned 24 administrative offices of a county government, employing 1,180 staff, to either reduce scheduled hours from 37.5 to 30 per week at full pay (12 offices) or continue on the standard schedule (12 offices) for nine months. Output was measured from administrative records, not from manager assessments, and actual hours from timesheets. The effect differed sharply by type of work. In case-processing offices, where work arrives as a backlog that can be cleared at any time, output per full-time employee changed by −2.1% (95% CI −6.8 to +2.6) relative to control and output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. In counter and contact-centre offices, where output depends on staff being present while the public is waiting, output per employee fell by 11.4% (95% CI −16.9 to −5.9), waiting times rose, and output per actual hour rose by a more modest 6.7%. Sick days fell by 29% across treated offices. An exploratory analysis suggests that a reduction in recurring meetings may account for part of the gain in case-processing offices.

## Motivation

Existing evidence on reduced working time comes mainly from voluntary pilots without comparison groups, in which output is often reported by the managers who sponsored the change. The county wished to know whether a reduced schedule could be extended to its own administrative staff without loss of service, and agreed to a randomised design with administrative output measures and a registered analysis plan.

## Design

**Units and randomisation.** The 24 offices were stratified into two strata by type of work before randomisation, and offices were randomised within strata:

- *Case-processing offices* (14 offices; 7 treated, 7 control): permits, licensing, benefits assessment and records. Work arrives as cases that join a queue and can be completed at any point within statutory deadlines.
- *Counter and contact-centre offices* (10 offices; 5 treated, 5 control): in-person service counters and telephone lines. Work arrives as members of the public who must be served while they wait.

Randomisation was at office level to avoid contamination between colleagues. Treated offices kept their public opening hours unchanged; staff rotas were rearranged so that each employee worked 30 scheduled hours.

**Outcomes.** The registered primary outcome is output per full-time-equivalent employee (FTE), measured as cases closed (case-processing) or contacts handled (counter and contact centre), from the county's case-management and telephony systems. Registered secondary outcomes are output per actual hour (from timesheets, which include any overtime claimed), quality (the share of decisions overturned on appeal; for contact centres, the repeat-contact rate within seven days), average waiting time, and sick days. Analysis is difference-in-differences against the six-month pre-period, with standard errors clustered by office.

**Exploratory measures.** At the request of office managers we also collected calendar data on recurring meetings in month six. This was not part of the registered plan.

## Results

### Hours

Scheduled hours fell by 20% in treated offices. Actual hours, from timesheets, fell by less: by 13% in case-processing offices (from 37.9 to 33.0 per week) and by 17% in counter offices (from 37.6 to 31.2), the difference reflecting overtime claimed to clear backlogs in case-processing. Control offices' actual hours were stable.

### Output and quality

**Table 1. Difference-in-differences estimates at nine months, treated relative to control**

| Outcome | Case-processing (7 v 7 offices) | Counter and contact centre (5 v 5 offices) |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −11.4% (−16.9 to −5.9) |
| Actual hours per FTE | −13% | −17% |
| Output per actual hour | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +6.7% (+0.4 to +13.3) |
| Appeal overturn rate / repeat contact rate | 3.1% v 3.0% | 11.8% v 10.9% |
| Average wait (minutes), treated offices, pre → month 9 | — | 4.2 → 6.9 |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% (both strata pooled) | |

In case-processing offices, output per employee was statistically indistinguishable from control, with a point estimate slightly below zero, and quality was unchanged. Because actual hours fell by 13%, output per actual hour rose by 12.5%. Measured against scheduled rather than actual hours, the gain would appear as 22%; we regard that figure as misleading, because staff did not in fact work only the scheduled hours.

In counter and contact-centre offices, the picture is different. With the same number of staff each working fewer hours, fewer staff were present at any given time during unchanged opening hours. Contacts handled per employee fell by 11.4% and the average wait rose from 4.2 to 6.9 minutes. Output per actual hour rose by 6.7%, but this did not offset the loss of hours, and the service the public received was worse. Abandoned calls rose from 6% to 10% of calls.

### Wellbeing

Sick days fell by 29% in treated offices relative to control. Resignations were lower in treated offices (annualised 3.9% against 7.4%), though with 12 offices per arm and few resignations the estimate is imprecise.

### Exploratory: meetings

Calendar data in month six showed that staff in treated case-processing offices spent 3.8 hours per week in recurring meetings against 7.1 hours in control case-processing offices, a difference of 3.3 hours. Offices that cut meetings most showed the largest gains in output per hour (correlation across the 7 treated offices, r = 0.71). Interviews suggested that the reduced schedule prompted managers to cancel standing meetings that had persisted by habit.

We emphasise that this analysis was not registered, that it rests on seven offices, and that a correlation across seven offices cannot establish a mechanism. We report it because, if confirmed, it would mean that a substantial part of the per-hour gain comes from removing low-value time rather than from rest alone, and that would matter for how the result is interpreted and for what other employers could expect. We have registered a confirmatory test for the 24-month follow-up.

## Discussion

Three conclusions follow from the registered analyses.

First, in work where output is not tied to presence, a 20% cut in scheduled hours produced a much smaller cut in actual hours and little or no measurable loss of output per employee. Output per hour rose by about an eighth.

Second, in work where output is tied to presence, the same change reduced output per employee by about a tenth and worsened service, even though each hour worked was somewhat more productive. Gains per hour do not by themselves imply that the hours reduction pays for itself. The question "does a shorter week raise productivity?" therefore has at least two answers depending on whether productivity is understood per hour or per employee, and these come apart most sharply in coverage-bound work.

Third, estimates computed against scheduled hours materially overstate the per-hour gain. In our data the overstatement is from 12.5% to 22% in case-processing offices.

These findings qualify claims, made on the basis of uncontrolled pilots, that reduced hours are sector-general. A sector may contain both kinds of work; what matters is whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence.

## Limitations

The trial is in one public employer, with 24 offices; confidence intervals are correspondingly wide, particularly in the counter stratum. Staff knew their assignment, and control staff knew that a trial was under way, which could have affected effort in either direction. Nine months may be too short to reveal whether gains persist after the novelty of the change wears off, or whether backlogs build up beyond the statutory deadlines. Public-sector case processing may differ from private-sector knowledge work in ways that affect the result. A 24-month follow-up is under way.

response:
This is a much stronger study than the previous working paper, and most of its conclusions are supported. The arithmetic checks out. The design avoids the pilot's main weaknesses: it is randomised, measures output from administrative records and actual hours from timesheets, and pre-registers its outcomes. The authors are also careful in the right places, refusing the 22% scheduled-hours figure and labelling the meetings analysis as exploratory. Most of the remaining issues concern how much precision to claim and a few gaps in reporting, not the direction of the findings. One point (§5 below) is worth adding because it strengthens the authors' own exploratory finding.

## What checks out

- **Actual hours:** 37.9→33.0 is −12.9%, and 37.6→31.2 is −17.0%.
- **Output per actual hour:** 0.979 / 0.871 gives +12.4–12.5% for case-processing. 0.886 / 0.830 gives +6.7% for counter offices.
- **Scheduled-hours comparison:** 0.979 / 0.8 = 1.224, so +22%, as stated.
- **Per-hour CIs:** they are roughly what you get by dividing the per-FTE CIs by the hours ratio, so they are internally consistent.
- **The primary outcome is reported first** and honestly, including the counter-stratum loss.

## Issues worth raising

### 1. Few clusters, so the CIs are probably too narrow

Standard errors are clustered by office, with only 14 clusters in one stratum and 10 in the other (5 v 5). Conventional cluster-robust SEs are known to be too optimistic with this few clusters. Wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference would be more appropriate. Randomisation inference is especially natural here, since the randomisation was stratified and its scheme is known exactly. The counter-stratum CI (−16.9 to −5.9) is the most likely to widen. The direction will probably survive, but the paper's stated precision may not.

### 2. "Differed sharply by type of work" needs a formal test

The Summary's headline claim is that the effect differs between strata, but no test of the difference is reported. The two per-FTE CIs actually overlap slightly: −6.8 in case-processing against −5.9 in counter offices. Overlapping intervals don't rule out a real difference, but the claim needs either a stratum-by-treatment interaction estimate or a statement that stratum-specific effects were the registered analysis. Stratifying the randomisation suggests they were, but the paper should say so explicitly.

### 3. Backlogs are measurable now, and they matter for the case-processing result

The defining feature of case-processing work is that it can be deferred. A −2.1% change in cases closed could therefore sit alongside a growing queue. The Limitations section treats deadline breaches as a future risk. But backlog size, time-to-decision, and the share of cases near or past statutory deadlines should all be available now from the same case-management system. Without them, "little or no measurable loss" applies to throughput, not to service.

Two related points:

- **Case mix.** Counting closures doesn't show whether easier cases were cleared first.
- **Appeal timing.** Appeals take months to resolve, so overturn rates at month nine mostly reflect decisions made early in the trial.

### 4. Timesheets may still undercount hours

The authors rightly argue that scheduled hours overstate per-hour gains. The same logic goes one step further. Timesheets record overtime that was *claimed*. Unclaimed work, such as salaried staff finishing cases at home or arriving early, wouldn't appear. Any such undercount inflates the 12.5% gain in the same way scheduled hours inflate it to 22%. A sentence acknowledging this, plus any system-login or case-activity timestamps if available, would close the gap.

### 5. Arithmetically, meetings could account for nearly all of the case-processing per-hour gain

This is the most interesting point, and it supports the authors' exploratory analysis.

- **Hours removed versus meeting time removed.** Treated case-processing staff cut actual hours by about 4.9 per week. They spent 3.3 fewer hours per week in meetings than control staff.
- **Non-meeting hours.** Suppose control meeting time (7.1 hours) approximates the treated offices' pre-trial level. Then non-meeting hours fell only from about 30.8 to 29.2, roughly −5%.
- **Output per non-meeting hour.** That works out to 0.979 / 0.948, about +3%.

On that rough accounting, most of the "per-hour productivity gain" is time moved out of meetings rather than faster work during the remaining hours. If confirmed, this has two implications:

- Rest and fatigue may play a smaller role than the general literature assumes.
- Much of the gain might be obtainable by cutting meetings without cutting hours.

The 24-month confirmatory test should pre-specify this decomposition.

One caveat on the exploratory analysis: calendar data were collected only in month six. "Offices that cut meetings most" implies a pre-period baseline, which the Design section doesn't mention. If no baseline exists, the r = 0.71 relates meeting *levels*, not *cuts*, to per-hour gains. The authors should clarify this. The treated-versus-control difference of 3.3 hours remains a valid randomised comparison either way.

### 6. The counter-office per-hour gain is probably mostly utilisation

With demand fixed and fewer staff present, each staff member spends less time idle between contacts. Longer waits and more abandoned calls show the queue absorbing the difference. A per-hour rise is the expected mechanical result of that, not evidence that people worked faster. The authors already conclude that per-hour gains don't mean the change pays for itself. Saying explicitly that the counter per-hour figure largely reflects queueing would strengthen that conclusion. Treated offices' higher repeat-contact rate (11.8% v 10.9%, if I read the table correctly) may also add slightly to "contacts handled."

### 7. Reporting inconsistencies in Table 1 and the Wellbeing section

The table mixes difference-in-differences estimates with raw comparisons, and several rows lack the information needed to interpret them:

- **Quality row.** It gives two levels ("3.1% v 3.0%") without saying which is treated, and it isn't a difference-in-differences estimate.
- **Waiting times and abandoned calls.** These are reported only for treated offices, pre versus month nine. They need the control trend.
- **Sick days and resignations.** These have no confidence intervals. Resignations are compared as levels (3.9% v 7.4%), not as a difference-in-differences estimate.

Bringing these onto the same basis as the primary outcome would make the table consistent.

### 8. Cost isn't reported

The county's question was whether the schedule could be extended "without loss of service." Two cost facts bear directly on that:

- **Case-processing offices:** they averaged about 3 hours per week of claimed overtime above the 30-hour schedule, presumably paid at a premium.
- **Counter offices:** restoring coverage would need roughly 20% more staff.

Cost per case and cost per contact are the natural decision measures, and they seem computable from data already held.

## Minor points

- **"Statistically indistinguishable from control"** is accurate, but "little or no measurable loss" in the Discussion is a bit generous. The CI still includes a 6.8% loss, which would matter operationally.
- **Contamination:** the Limitations section notes that control staff knew about the trial. Resentment or demoralisation in control offices would inflate the estimated effect, so it's worth saying which direction the authors think is more likely.

## In relation to the previous paper

This study effectively tests the Halden pilot's weak points and confirms them:

| Halden pilot claim | What this trial found |
|---|---|
| Per-hour gain of +23% | Scheduled-hours framing inflates the gain from 12.5% to 22% |
| "Sector-general" | Coverage-bound work loses output and service |
| Gains in all sectors | The per-hour figure in coverage work largely reflects queueing |

The authors' framing in the Discussion, distinguishing work by "whether output in a given role depends on hours of presence" rather than by sector, is the right one and a genuine contribution.

I can draft a revised Table 1, sketch the randomisation-inference analysis, or write up the meetings decomposition as a pre-registration note for the 24-month follow-up.
